One of the big points of voat seems to be to do one thing, just like reddit. Voat serves the purpose of creating a "item" and then ranking that item among many others, based on different categories. Secondly, they serve to create communities around which these items are created and shared.

The current system consists of making the website into what is basically a whole bunch of "mini-websites" where there is some moderator or admin who has total control over that "mini-site". This is bad because it allows people to squat on domains, delete and censor comments as they see fit, and to remove and shut down user discussion.

One solution to this could be to have some sort of democracy system, where users can vote against and bring down moderators, admins, and so on. However, that results in the issue of shutting down the ability for a community to form. Decentralizing the mini-site allows for external communities to come into existing ones and shut them down/shut them up.

A system that should work would allow all people to freely and openly discuss, but still allows users to see good content and discussion. This could be done with simply using activity, rather than using negative vs positive reaction, but that causes trolls and other comments that incite large reactions to become large and rise to the top (see, google's system).

Systems for showing people what they want to see need to not be based on direct user interaction. If this is true, then users can game the system. However, users need to be able to feel like they are accomplishing something at the same time. The upvoat and downvoat system also fails here, since it allows people to attempt to hide the things they don't like, even in the absence of mods and so on.

The best system, in my opinion, would be one which categorizes and sorts posts based on user history and interactions. Lets say there is a person A that always upvotes photos of space, but really hates photos of dogs, and this person always downvotes images of dogs.

Now, lets say there is another person, who loves dogs, and always upvotes them, and loves space, and always upvotes images of space.

The first line of separation on voat would be some form of "streams". A stream is a source of content that you can subscribe or not subscribe to. Streams would be composed of the activities of many communities. Lets say there is a "dogs" stream. This stream would be the result of all the different places where animals are posted, and contain every image where a large number of people in each community tagged an image with "dog". Over time, as a community posts and uses more and more tags, it will come "closer" to a different stream, and snap to any specific one.

So, a stream would be "animals" while communities would be "cats" "dogs", and so on. Then you would need substreams or merging streams, so animals could contain all the different streams of content, so there can be a dog substream to animals.

Communities, in this case, would be the hardest thing to manage well, and ultimately their design would be the foundation for how voat really wants to run. A community could be very inclusive, able to kick out users by disliking them, or a community could be based on activity, where those dedicated to a place are allowed to continue to post there.

The average users wouldn't see the communities, or any of the streams-substreams-metadata organization. They would simply join and see a list of "content groups" of which they can select what they like, and see posts coming in. Eventually, they will naturally want to curate what they see, and can start cutting out "substreams" from what they like, banning dogs from animals, for instance. Eventually, as a user posts in and interacts with people in different streams, they unlock or gain access to the communities behind them, and gain the ability to posts from within those communities.

Community members who make posts in their community will not see the reactions to their posts outside of their community, when the posts enter the stream. They will be able to go and see the reactions, but they will be unable to see it if they do not themselves go to see it. Any users who comment on a post that has left the community will not be able to see or identify the original community the post came from, to prevent the braiding or attacking of communities by others.

Communities will be formed as subvoats are today, and users will be either able to post regularly to a stream, or to a community.

Any thoughts? This was a ten minute writeup/brainstorm, so it isn't too well thought out, but it is a possible system that could deal with some of the issues inherent to reddit-like systems.

Streams would be the equivalent of a "large" subverse where there is no sense of community. They would function as the defaults do currently on reddit. You would manage and control streams exactly as you do with subverses now. As for managing your own, that's where you form and start inviting people into a community. Subverses are for the "average" user, whereas communities are for the active and frequently posting ones.

Of course, a community can be as open or closed as someone wants to make it.

This makes it so that communities cannot shut down the flow of information. If someone is subscribed to a stream, they get content from many communities, many cultures, etc, and it keeps one moderator from shutting down something because they don't like it. If people want to see something, they can see it in a stream. If they do not, they can cut out these subverses from the streams that have content they do not want to see.

So the chain of info would go as such

Community -> strict moderation based on a variable system, easy ability to curate who can join, can be controlled by one user as a mod, or by democracy, with options to start the community as either.

Substream -> communities connect here, and all info to a substream is somewhat specific. A community with a popular post with the tag of "dog" and "cute" will go into the animals and the aww substreams. No users have control directly.

Stream -> A stream is a large collection of substream posts, which are created, again, by users tagging a stream with substreams they think are relavent. No users have control over these directly.

A new user sees the most abstract, and least controlled, field of play. The mods cannot control or censor any info.

As a user browses more, they learn of substreams, and learn they can hide some of them, and curate info.

Then they start getting into communities, and start participating in them, producing content.

You can't grow past what reddit's problems are now without changing the system in a drastic way. If you could, reddit would have done it already. Reddit can't change drastically without massive user loss. Voat may be able to.
